summary: Deep technical session focused on architecture-specific tuning for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen style models. Discussed KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs (4-bit vs 8-bit), MoE routing costs and implications, and RoPE scaling/compatibility. Agreed to run benchmarks with customer's prompt set and share a cost/latency spreadsheet; follow-up to review MoE economics and VPC/on-prem constraints.
topics: MoE routing costs and sparsity tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00:00] Sarah Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna do a technical deep dive on model arch tuning, focusing on Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and some MoE/rope specifics. michelle sorry mic drop, i mean miguel you'll kick off with latency stuff.
[00:00:12] Miguel Torres: Yeah so hi all, thanks. quick agenda: baseline throughput/latency, kv cache interactions, batching, quant, then moE and RoPE. i'll start with a quick baseline: for autoregressive workloads with 1k tokens, continuous batching helps but you hit diminishing returns after ~8-16 concurrent requests depending on sequence length. on A100s we typically see Mistral-7B at ~65 tps when using fp16, drop to ~48 tps for 8-bit quant at similar latency targets.
[00:00:45] Alex Rivera: When you say "8-bit quant" do you mean QAT or post training quant? and what toolchain are you using, bitsandbytes?
[00:00:52] Miguel Torres: mostly PTQ with per-channel scales, some models we do QAT for sensitive layers. yes bitsandbytes for the 4/8-bit backends but we also validate with custom kernels in our runtime. there's a quality delta for some attention layers, esp on Llama-style models.
[00:01:10] Jenna Park: Quick infra question: if we go dedicated or on-prem, does the KV cache persist between requests or is it per-session only? we have a lot of short interactive sessions.
[00:01:20] Priya Kapoor: by default KV cache is in-memory on the worker and keyed by session id; for interactive apps you can keep long-lived sessions to amortize KV compute. we also support prefix caching which can be shared across users for common prompts but watch out for memory pressure. on Dedicated we give you options to increase KV cache memory per replica.
[00:01:39] Omar Patel: any quant impact on KV cache size?
[00:01:42] Miguel Torres: good Q — quant primarily reduces model weights memory; KV cache is activations, so size is mostly seq_len * hidden_size * 2 for fp16; with 8-bit activation quant we can shave some but activation quant is riskier for generation. so in practice KV cache remains the big memory consumer for long sequences.
[00:01:58] Alex Rivera: let's talk RoPE. we've seen degenerations when scaling context -like hallucinations or repetition. is that RoPE related?
[00:02:05] Priya Kapoor: sometimes yes. RoPE scaling issues can arise with different positional freq embeddings; some open models use scaled RoPE (alibi-like adjustments) to extend context. for Llama-family you might see rotary artifacts at extreme lengths. we recommend model-specific tuning: enabling position interpolation or using our fallback to chunking + overlap for >8k contexts.
[00:02:26] Miguel Torres: also a note: for Qwen we've seen that RoPE implementations differ slightly which affects KV cache indexing; when we fallback to a compatible variant, we sometimes need to recompile kernels which adds warmup time.
[00:02:40] Jenna Park: about MoE — we're experimenting with an internal MoE. concern is routing overheads and idle expert cost. what should we watch for?
[00:02:48] Miguel Torres: MoE routing costs are twofold: compute for the router and the sparsely-activated experts themselves. network IO matters if experts are sharded across devices; routing can be cheap for small models but as you scale experts across hosts, you pay communication and scheduling. our runtime supports co-located experts and model parallel routing to minimize cross-host traffic, but if you need on-prem with limited NVLink you might hit latency spikes.
[00:03:10] Alex Rivera: can you quantify that? like how much tail latency increase?
[00:03:14] Miguel Torres: ballpark: intra-host MoE routing adds ~3-8ms per token; cross-host can add 15-50ms depending on network and batch. it's workload dependent — for high-batch throughput the overhead amortizes, for low-latency single-query SLOs it's more costly.
[00:03:30] Sarah Chen: is that also true for Qwen-MoE variants?
[00:03:34] Priya Kapoor: yes, Qwen-MoE routing is similar but their router tends to select fewer experts which reduces compute but can increase variance; Llama-MoE prototypes we've tested had higher memory moves. Mistral hasn't widely released MoE variants, but architecture differences can change routing arithmetic.
[00:03:50] Jenna Park: regarding batching: we have a strict 200ms p95 SLO for chat responses. what's the recommended batching config?
[00:03:58] Miguel Torres: for a 200ms p95 target we recommend shallow batching: max batch size 4-8, request queuing window 10-30ms, and adaptive policies to avoid queuing under low load. also enable prefix caching; that gives you big wins when many requests share prompts. quantify in our benchmark: with prefix cache on a 1k token workload, p95 dropped from 420ms to 210ms for Llama2-13B under moderate concurrency.
[00:04:22] Alex Rivera: any artifacts from compilation/kernel selection? we saw weird spikes after loading a new model.
[00:04:28] Priya Kapoor: yes that’s usually JIT/compilation warmup: first few requests trigger kernel compiles and memory allocations. we have warmup hooks (preload key kernels) and also recommend a smoke-run of representative prompts during deployment; for private/on-prem you can run a synthetic warmup job. we also keep compiled kernels cached on disk for faster restarts.
[00:04:47] Omar Patel: about quant-induced quality regressions: how do you measure and detect them automatically?
[00:04:51] Miguel Torres: we use eval suites tied to prompts — BLEU-like for structured tasks, embedding similarity for semantic tasks, plus human-in-the-loop spot checks. Redwood Optimize can run regression alerts if metric drops exceed thresholds. for subtle hallucination shifts, you need targeted evals; automated diffs help, but human review is often needed.
[00:05:08] Alex Rivera: are there specific layers you avoid quantizing?
[00:05:11] Priya Kapoor: feed-forward and attention projection layers are safer to quantize; the first and last layers, and sometimes LayerNorm scales, are often left fp16 or fp32. we document per-model recommended profiles; we'll share the Mistral/Llama/Qwen guides.
[00:05:25] Sarah Chen: we captured a couple of questions earlier about private deployments. Jenna, any constraints for on-prem?
[00:05:30] Jenna Park: data residency and isolated networking is required. basically VPC-only, no external internet egress, HSM for keys if possible. also we have limited NVSwitch so multi-host MoE might not be viable.
[00:05:42] Miguel Torres: that matches our experience — for on-prem with limited interconnect, prefer co-located experts or smaller MoE configurations. or use dedicated capacity in a cloud region with NVLink for heavy MoE. we can produce a routing-cost model comparing options.
[00:05:55] Alex Rivera: can you share a concrete benchmark sheet?
[00:05:58] Priya Kapoor: yes, Miguel will run the benchmarks and we'll share a spreadsheet ("NSAI-MODEL-BENCH-0304.xlsx") and a short doc on quant profiles; link will be shared in slack.
[00:06:06] Sarah Chen: let's get into a quick example: Llama2-13B vs Mistral-7B for chat loads with 1k context, 200ms p95 goal.
[00:06:13] Miguel Torres: sure. in our internal tests: with fp16, Llama2-13B needs ~1.6x the GPU memory and gives similar latency to Mistral-7B but slightly higher token quality on some instruction tasks. after 4-bit quant, Mistral-7B often wins for cost due to better density but watch for 1-2% accuracy drops on edge evals. for p95 200ms you'd likely pick Mistral with shallow batching and prefix cache if throughput is modest.
[00:06:36] Jenna Park: what about Qwen-14B?
[00:06:39] Miguel Torres: Qwen-14B sits between 13B and 20B semantic quality; it has a different attention matmul memory profile which can affect KV cache layout. quantization tends to be decent but RoPE differences require kernel compatibility checks.
[00:06:53] Alex Rivera: we run some long form summarization; 8k-16k contexts. best practice?
[00:06:58] Priya Kapoor: chunking with overlap + stateful KV is common. for 16k prefer models that explicitly support long RoPE scaling or provide position interpolation. otherwise you get position collapse. also monitor KV cache memory and enable eviction heuristics for long-running sessions.
[00:07:14] Miguel Torres: one more note on batching + SLOs: our runtime supports qos-based scheduling: you can tag critical requests to skip batching or use a priority lane. that helps keep p95 low while still achieving throughput on background jobs.
[00:07:27] Omar Patel: any gotchas for mixed-precision on older GPUs?
[00:07:30] Miguel Torres: yes older cards may not have fast fp16 matrix ops; quant kernels might be slower. in those cases 8-bit or even fp32 might be better for latency. we can surface hardware recommendations in our benchmark report.
[00:07:41] Alex Rivera: follow-ups: can you estimate cost delta for MoE versus dense for our workload?
[00:07:45] Priya Kapoor: we'll model it — rough rule: MoE reduces FLOPs for same quality but increases variance in latency and memory patterns. if you have high batch throughput and tolerant latency SLOs, MoE often wins on cost; for strict p95 it can be worse. we'll produce a per-configuration estimate in the benchmark sheet.
[00:08:02] Sarah Chen: ok, let's capture next steps. Miguel will run the bench, Priya will assemble MoE/rope notes, Jenna will upload prompt set. any other stakeholders?
[00:08:12] Alex Rivera: please include our infra lead and procurement when you share the quote.
[00:08:16] Sarah Chen: noted. we'll also include a short playbook for on-prem warmups and kernel precompilation.
[00:08:22] Miguel Torres: i'll add a section on kernel selection heuristics and warmup commands.
[00:08:26] Sarah Chen: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with a recording and the benchmark link.
[00:08:32] Alex Rivera: thanks all.
[00:08:35] Jenna Park: thanks.
[00:08:36] [END]
